issues.legal_issue: Giving an undertaking to comply temporarily with an adverse order does not bar an appeal under the constitutional special-leave jurisdiction.
material_facts: After the High Court dismissed the tenant’s revision, it granted time to vacate on condition that the tenant file an undertaking to do so.
The tenant filed the undertaking and then appealed by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The appeal could not be dismissed as not maintainable merely because the tenant had given the undertaking. The tenant remained bound by it while the order was operative, subject to any stay or change ordered by a superior court.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of election or estoppel cannot foreclose a statutory appeal or a constitutional remedy. Complying with an undertaking given to obtain temporary relief does not itself amount to giving up the right to challenge the order. The Court relied on Evans v. Bartlam and distinguished the approach in R. N. Gosain v. Yashpal Dhir and Vidhi Shanker v. Heera Lal, Ramchandra Jai Ram Randive v. Chandanmal Rupchand, and Thacker Hariram Motiram v. Balkrishan Chatrabhu Thacker.

predicates.constitutional_special_leave_appeal: A party brings a constitutional appeal by special leave from an adverse order.
predicates.undertaking_given_to_obtain_temporary_re: The party gives an undertaking to obtain temporary relief from the effect of the adverse order.

issues.definition: When a party brings a constitutional special-leave appeal after giving an undertaking to obtain temporary relief, the undertaking does not bar the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant must pay or deposit the arrears of rent required by law when filing a rent-control revision, unless the statutory procedure for resolving a dispute about the amount applies.
material_facts: The tenant filed a revision challenging an eviction order without depositing the arrears of rent.
The High Court noted that no rent had been deposited when the revision was filed.
The tenant argued that the obligation to deposit arose only after the court determined the amount, but the judgment identified that determination procedure as applying where the amount was disputed.
issues.conclusion: The revision was not maintainable because the tenant had not paid or deposited the arrears when filing it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29(1) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act requires payment or deposit of all arrears due when a tenant prefers a revision, and continued payment or deposit of rent becoming due during the proceedings. Section 29(3) provides for a summary determination where there is a dispute about the amount; it does not postpone the initial obligation where no such dispute is raised. Section 29(4) provides for stopping proceedings and directing possession or dismissing the revision in case of failure, unless sufficient cause is shown.

predicates.rent_control_revision: A tenant brings a revision in a rent-control proceeding against an eviction order.
predicates.arrears_unpaid_or_undeposited_when_filed: The tenant has not paid or deposited the arrears due when filing the revision.

issues.definition: When a tenant brings a rent-control revision without paying or depositing the arrears due at filing, the revision is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A contention that later payment cured the failure to deposit arrears when filing a revision need not be considered when it was not raised in the lower proceeding or in the special-leave petition.
material_facts: The tenant contended before the Supreme Court that later payment of the arrears should mean the revision was treated as filed on the date of that payment.
The tenant had not raised that ground in response to the landlord’s application before the District Court or in the special-leave petition.
The landlord had therefore had no opportunity to meet the factual basis of the contention.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the contention in this case.
issues.legal_principle: A factual contention may be declined when it was not raised in the proceeding below or in the petition bringing the matter to the Supreme Court, leaving the opposing party without an opportunity to respond. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and later_payment_claimed_to_cure_initial_omission and claim_not_raised_below and claim_not_in_appeal_petition

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party brings an appeal before the Supreme Court from an adverse order.
predicates.later_payment_claimed_to_cure_initial_om: The party claims that a later payment cured a failure to pay or deposit an amount when required earlier.
predicates.claim_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the contention in the relevant lower-court proceeding.
predicates.claim_not_in_appeal_petition: The party did not include the contention in the petition bringing the matter to the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a contention that later payment cured an earlier omission is not considered when it was raised neither below nor in the appeal petition.
